To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability of adults to select task relevant visual stimuli in a complex scene depends on both reflexive and voluntary mechanisms of attention, while children are only able to use voluntary mechanisms to guide their attention to relevant stimuli.

(1) the orienting effect, indicating the capture of spatial attention to the location of an auditory cue, is independent of age, (2) the reorienting effects, indicating the suppression of the orienting effect by a target, are only present in adults, and (3) the searching performance is predicted by task related saliencies (TgS and NSL) in adults but not in children

children and adults show a comparable orienting of spatial attention by auditory cues, but only adults demonstrate a suppression of the orienting of spatial to a task relevant target following distraction by a task irrelevant cue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of selective attention in the visual search of complex scenes.

how children's attentional mechanisms develop from childhood to adulthood, and in particular, the interplay between two attentional processes that are known to be involved in visual search: voluntary and reflexive attention.
the study of selective attention during the search for a target in a complex visual scene, in the presence of a task irrelevant auditory stimulus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

voluntary mechanisms of selective attention (e.g. the use of target saliency) develop late in childhood and are only fully functional in early adulthood, whereas reflexive mechanisms (e.g. spatial orienting by salient stimuli) are fully functional in childhood.
the voluntary mechanisms are already mature in childhood and the reflexive ones develop in adolescence.
the voluntary control of attention develops with age, while the reflexive capture of attention does not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of voluntary control of selective attention is a late process that occurs during early adulthood.
the interplay between reflexive and volitional mechanisms of selective attention is not fully developed until early adulthood.
children are less capable of inhibiting the capture of reflexive attention and of selecting task relevant saliency, compared to adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children show a stronger attraction of processing resources by task irrelevant locations and a weaker use of task relevant perceptually salient information than adults.
the mechanisms that support the selection of task-relevant stimuli during visual search are qualitatively different in adults and in children.
children's and adults' attentional mechanisms differ in terms of the interplay of reflexive and voluntary mechanisms.
